summary: Assigns the fixed pseudowire identifier and other fixed protocol values for protocols defined in the Pseudo Wire Edge to Edge (PWE3) working group, and gives IANA detailed allocation instructions. It is a Best Current Practice document.

eli5.summary: A list that gives each pseudowire code its own number, so nobody uses the same number for two different things.

questions: what is a pseudowire type identifier
subtitle: Assigns identifier numbers for pseudowire protocols to prevent conflicts.

tldr.problem: Multiple protocols for emulating wired circuits over IP networks (Ethernet, ATM, Frame Relay) need globally unique identifiers to avoid confusion.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4446 creates IANA registries and allocates fixed numeric identifiers for each pseudowire protocol type, interface parameter, attachment identifier, and status code.
tldr.outcome: Networks can unambiguously identify which circuit emulation protocol is in use on each pseudowire connection.

today: RFC 4446 is a Best Current Practice document and remains the authoritative source for PWE3 IANA allocations. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
PWE3 (Pseudowire Edge to Edge Emulation) is a set of protocols that lets network operators send traditional circuit signals—like phone lines, leased lines, Ethernet, and ATM—over modern packet networks using MPLS. Each pseudowire protocol needs a unique numeric identifier so equipment from different vendors can recognize what protocol is being used.

RFC 4446 defines the IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) registries that assign these identifiers. The registries use three allocation policies: IETF consensus for core protocols, expert review for emerging ones, and first-come-first-served for proprietary extensions.
sections.eli5: Think of it like a phone system: each type of signal (voice, data, video) needs its own line number so the phone company and customers agree on what is being sent.

sections.title: Pseudowire Type Registry
sections.content:
The main registry allocates 15-bit pseudowire type identifiers. Values 1 through 30 are assigned in RFC 4446 itself, covering common circuit types: Frame Relay, ATM (multiple variants), Ethernet (tagged and untagged), HDLC, PPP, SONET/SDH circuit emulation, and TDM over packet networks. Each type has a one-line description and a reference to the RFC that defines it.

Values 31 through 1024 are reserved for future protocols needing expert review. Values 1025 through 4096 and 32767 go through IETF consensus. Values 4097 through 32766 are reserved for vendor proprietary extensions, allocated first-come-first-served.
sections.eli5: The numbers 1 to 30 are already taken by standard signal types. New standard types get numbers 31 to 1024 (if experts say OK). Vendors can use the high numbers (4097 to 32766) for their own secret sauce.

sections.title: Interface Parameters and Identifiers
sections.content:
Beyond the pseudowire type, the RFC defines sub-registries for optional parameters that describe a pseudowire connection. Interface Parameter Sub-TLV types (8-bit values 1 to 12) specify things like maximum transmission unit (MTU) in octets, interface description strings, payload byte counts for TDM circuits, bit rates, and VLAN IDs. Status code bits (32 bits) indicate operational state: whether the pseudowire is forwarding, and whether there are local faults on the ingress, egress, or far-end sides.

Attachment Identifier registries assign unique identifiers to the connection points. Attachment Individual Identifier (AII) Type 1 is a 32-bit number identifying one endpoint. Attachment Group Identifier (AGI) Type 1 is an 8-byte value encoded as a Route Distinguisher, grouping multiple pseudowires together.
sections.eli5: Just like a packet header says source and destination, a pseudowire connection needs to say whether it is working, broken, or sleeping. The parameters are extra labels for how big the connection is and what kind of circuit it emulates.

sections.title: Allocation Policies
sections.content:
RFC 4446 defines three policies for assigning new identifiers. IETF consensus (highest bar) applies to core protocol values and ensures broad agreement. Expert review (medium bar) applies to new circuit emulation methods: an expert must approve each request within 10 business days, checking for duplication, clear descriptions, and correct value ranges. First-come-first-served (lowest bar) applies to vendor proprietary values: vendors get a number on request, but vendor proprietary types MUST NOT be used in IETF standards.

The document notes that value zero is always reserved and must never be used in any registry.
sections.eli5: Like a patent office: big decisions (standards) need committee approval. Medium ones (new inventions) need a specialist to review. Vendor codes are fast-track, but cannot be mixed into the standards.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC allocates only numeric identifiers, not the protocols that carry the pseudowired traffic. The document states explicitly that security properties depend on the protocols that use these identifiers, not on the identifiers themselves. Each protocol (Frame Relay transport, Ethernet encapsulation, SONET emulation, and so on) handles its own security requirements. RFC 4446 does not add or remove any security guarantees.
sections.eli5: The number itself is not the security—it is just a label. The real safety is in how each circuit type is built, and that is handled by other RFCs.
